content: The effectiveness of decongestants, antihistamines, and nasal irrigation in children diagnosed with acute sinusitis has not been systematically studied. The objective of this research was to evaluate whether these treatments improve symptoms in children with acute sinusitis. To gather relevant data, searches were conducted in CENTRAL (up to Issue 5, 2014), MEDLINE (from 1950 to the first week of June 2014), and EMBASE (from 1950 to June 2014). The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving children under 18 years of age who had acute sinusitis, defined as 10 to 30 days of rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, or daytime cough. Studies involving children with chronic sinusitis or allergic rhinitis were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion. Out of 662 studies identified through electronic searches and manual searching, none met all the inclusion criteria. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the efficacy of antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal irrigation in treating children with acute sinusitis. Further research is necessary to determine whether these interventions are beneficial for this condition.
